title: International Payment Costs Compared 2026: Razorpay vs Other Options on Fees, FX, GST and Minimums
summary: International payment cost is the difference between a comparable reference value for an overseas customer payment and the net amount your business receives.
body_markdown:
**International payment cost is the difference between a comparable reference value for an overseas customer payment and the net amount your business receives.** To compare Razorpay with other options, separate processing fees, the actual exchange rate, GST on taxable charges, minimum fees and other disclosed deductions. Use the same invoice size, currency and collection method.


An Indian consultant invoices a customer for USD 5,000. At an illustrative ₹95 per USD, that represents ₹4,75,000 before payment costs. The amount reaching the bank depends on how the customer pays and the terms that apply to that collection. A lower headline percentage does not settle the comparison by itself.


This guide explains Razorpay’s advertised card and bank-transfer fee structure, shows how invoice size affects a flat-charge example, and provides a consistent method for comparing actual quotes. Every exchange rate and worked scenario below is illustrative unless explicitly described as published pricing.


## Key Takeaways


- **Collect international card and bank-transfer payments in one place.** Razorpay brings both methods into one dashboard, helping businesses track overseas collections.
- **Invoice size affects the cost of bank transfers.** MoneySaver lists a flat ₹1,000 fee on transactions below ₹1,00,000, with GST applicable. A fixed charge makes up a larger share of a small invoice.
- **Separate currency conversion from payment charges.** Gross INR shows the conversion before fees; net INR shows what reaches your bank.
- **PA-CB payments have a ₹25 lakh limit per transaction.** This applies to payments processed by a PA-CB, rather than every overseas bank transfer.
- **Use cards for online checkout and bank transfers for invoices.** Cards let customers pay while buying online; bank transfers support invoice-based overseas collections.


## What Determines the All-In Cost?


The cost depends on the processing charge, conversion rate and other applicable deductions. These do not always use the same base. A replacement minimum should not be added to a percentage fee unless the tariff explicitly charges both.


Component What to obtain Common comparison mistake


Processing fee Rate, fee base, payment method and eligibility. Applying a domestic rate to international cards.


FX conversion Applied rate, currency pair, rate source and conversion time. Comparing a payment-time conversion with a later market rate.


Minimum or flat charge Threshold, replacement/additional treatment and tax. Adding a replacement minimum to the percentage charge.


GST Taxable service charges and the provider’s tax invoice. Treating the processor’s GST calculation as the tax treatment of the export invoice.


Other deductions Applicable correspondent, refund, dispute or optional-service charges. Assuming an unknown charge is either zero or definitely payable.


### A calculation that keeps the bases clear


Start with the converted payment rather than adding headline percentages:


1. **Gross converted INR:** foreign amount converted × applied conversion rate.
2. **Processing charge:** the quoted percentage applied to its stated base, or the applicable replacement flat charge.
3. **GST:** the applicable tax on taxable service charges; the illustrations here assume 18%.
4. **Net receipts:** gross converted INR minus processing charge, GST and other disclosed deductions.
5. **All-in effective cost:** reference conversion value minus net receipts, divided by reference conversion value, multiplied by 100.


For a like-for-like comparison, the reference conversion must use the same foreign amount, currency pair and relevant conversion time. Where fee bases differ, calculate rupee amounts first. Simply adding a fee percentage and an FX percentage may produce an inaccurate result.


> **Pro Tip:** Compare the gross conversion, processing fee, GST and final bank credit for the same invoice amount. This shows the full cost of collecting the payment.


## How Does Razorpay Price International Cards and Bank Transfers?


Razorpay’s[international-payments page](https://razorpay.com/accept-international-payments/) advertises card pricing up to 3% and bank-transfer pricing of 1%. The[pricing explainer](https://razorpay.com/blog/razorpay-payment-gateway-pricing-explained/) separates international cards from international bank transfers and describes GST on fees. The final cost depends on the payment method, invoice size, exchange rate and account pricing.


Razorpay collection method Published pricing reference What affects the final cost


International cards Up to 3% advertised processing fee; applicable GST is additional in the pricing explainer. Approved rate, fee base, card eligibility, conversion rate and other applicable charges.


MoneySaver bank transfers 1% advertised; bank-transfer page states zero FX markup and a ₹1,000 flat fee below ₹1,00,000, with GST applicable. Replacement versus additional fee treatment, covered flow, invoice size and actual conversion rate.

Card checkout suits customers who want to pay while purchasing. A bank-transfer collection account can suit invoiced B2B receipts where the customer can initiate a transfer. The[MoneySaver Export Account page](https://razorpay.com/accept-international-payments/bank-transfers/) explains the bank-transfer collection method and pricing.


### What does 18% GST on the processing fee mean?


For an illustrative ₹1,00,000 fee base, a 3% processing charge is ₹3,000. If 18% GST applies to that charge, tax is ₹540 and the combined deduction is ₹3,540. A 1% processing charge on the same base is ₹1,000 plus ₹180 GST, or ₹1,180.


These examples isolate the processor’s service charge. They do not establish the GST treatment of the underlying customer invoice or exclude tax on other applicable services.


## How Can a Flat Charge Change the Cost of a Small Invoice?


A flat charge represents a larger percentage of a small invoice. The following example uses a ₹1,000 flat fee instead of a 1% charge for invoices below ₹1 lakh. It shows how invoice size changes the effective cost.


This example assumes 18% GST on the processing charge, no other deductions and the same FX rate. Actual charges follow the applicable account pricing.


Invoice / fee base Modelled processing charge GST at 18% Total deduction Effective deduction


₹20,000 ₹1,000 flat ₹180 ₹1,180 5.90%


₹50,000 ₹1,000 flat ₹180 ₹1,180 2.36%


₹95,000 ₹1,000 flat ₹180 ₹1,180 1.2421%


₹1,00,000 ₹1,000 at 1% ₹180 ₹1,180 1.18%


₹4,75,000 ₹4,750 at 1% ₹855 ₹5,605 1.18%


### Where is the illustrative crossover against a 3% card fee?


Under identical FX and no-other-charge assumptions, a 3% card fee plus 18% GST produces a 3.54% deduction. Comparing that with a replacement flat fee of ₹1,000 plus ₹180 GST gives:


**Crossover invoice value = ₹1,180 ÷ 0.0354 = approximately ₹33,333.33.**


Below that value, the modelled percentage-based card charge is smaller. Above it, the modelled bank-transfer charge is smaller. Different FX, account terms or customer requirements can change the practical decision. The crossover applies to this example; different rates or charges change the result.


> **Did You Know?** A flat ₹1,180 deduction is 5.90% of ₹20,000 but about 1.24% of ₹95,000. The invoice size can change the effective rate even when the rupee charge is unchanged.


## How Do You Measure FX Markup Without Including Fees?


Use the gross converted amount before fees, GST and other deductions. Dividing the final bank credit by the foreign invoice amount gives a net receipt rate, which is useful for total-cost analysis but does not isolate FX.


**Illustration:** USD 1,000 converted at an assumed ₹95 gives ₹95,000 gross. Under the replacement-flat-fee assumption above, deduct ₹1,000 and ₹180 GST. Net credit is ₹93,820.


Dividing ₹93,820 by USD 1,000 gives ₹93.82 per USD. That does not mean the conversion rate was ₹93.82: this example used ₹95, with ₹1,180 deducted as fee and tax. Calling the full difference an FX markup would misstate the calculation.


### A practical FX check


1. Start with the foreign-currency amount converted.
2. Use the gross converted INR before deductions.
3. Divide gross INR by the foreign amount to calculate the applied rate.
4. Record the conversion timestamp and currency pair.
5. Compare with a reference rate for that same time and pair.
6. Reconcile processing charges, GST and other deductions separately.


Razorpay’s[currency-conversion documentation](https://razorpay.com/docs/payments/international-payments/currency-conversion) describes the processing bank’s rate at payment time for its standard gateway flow. Comparing that conversion with a later settlement-day rate can mix market movement with the spread. The conversion point depends on the collection method.


> **Pro Tip:** Use the applied exchange rate and its conversion time to measure FX costs. Without both figures, a difference in bank credit cannot be attributed to FX alone.


## Razorpay vs Other Options: A Fair Quote-Comparison Template


Compare actual quotes for the same use case. Broad market bands for wallets, wires or card gateways cannot reliably predict a specific Indian business’s net receipt. Consumer-remittance statistics also do not establish B2B invoice pricing.


Input Razorpay quote Other option’s quote


Product and collection method Record the approved method. Record the equivalent method or explain the difference.


Invoice amount and currency Use the same amount. Use the same amount.


Processing rate and base Enter the quoted rate and base. Enter the quoted rate and base.


Applied FX rate and time Enter the documented conversion. Enter the comparable conversion.


Minimum / flat fee Record threshold and replacement/additional treatment. Record threshold and replacement/additional treatment.


Tax and other charges Include applicable disclosed deductions. Use equivalent tax and charge assumptions.


Net received and timing Calculate the net credit and record when settlement starts. Calculate the net credit and record when settlement starts.


The comparison includes any intermediary-bank, refund, dispute or optional accelerated-settlement charges that apply. Costs that are not stated remain unknown rather than being treated as zero.


### The same USD 5,000 invoice, with declared assumptions


This illustration uses ₹95 per USD for both methods, a gross fee base of ₹4,75,000, 18% GST on the processing charge, and no other costs. It compares fee assumptions, not measured provider outcomes.


Line item 1% fee assumption 3% fee assumption


Gross converted INR ₹4,75,000 ₹4,75,000


Processing fee ₹4,750 ₹14,250


GST on fee ₹855 ₹2,565


Total deduction ₹5,605 ₹16,815


Net receipts ₹4,69,395 ₹4,58,185


The difference is ₹11,210 under those assumptions. It does not prove a saving for a real invoice if the customer cannot use both methods or the FX, pricing and other charges differ.


### Can a lower processing fee be outweighed by FX?


It can, depending on the FX markup. In a simplified same-base illustration, 1% processing plus 2% FX plus GST of 0.18% on the processing fee totals 3.18%. That is below a 3% processing fee plus 0.54% GST, which totals 3.54%. It would be incorrect to claim the first example is more expensive. Actual calculations must reflect whether the processing fee is applied before or after conversion.


## How Does GST Apply to These Costs?


The GST charged on a provider’s taxable processing service is separate from the tax treatment of your sale to the overseas customer. For the processing-fee examples here, 18% GST applies to the assumed taxable charge. Other banking or conversion services may have different taxable bases.


The limited exemption discussed in CBIC’s payment-aggregator clarification concerns the settlement function for qualifying card transactions up to ₹2,000. It does not create a blanket exemption for payment-gateway services.


Export zero-rating depends on the relevant statutory conditions. An LUT is a route for eligible exports without payment of IGST, rather than the only route. GST registration alone does not establish input-tax-credit eligibility for every charge. The provider’s tax invoice records GST on its charges; the export invoice and input-credit position are separate parts of the business’s tax records.


## Export and Import Collections Use Different Terms


An Indian business collecting from an overseas customer is considering an export collection. A non-Indian business accepting payments from Indian customers is considering a different import-side product and onboarding flow. Do not transfer a price between them merely because both involve international payments.


Razorpay’s[import-flow documentation](https://razorpay.com/docs/payments/international-payments/accept-international-payments-from-indian-customers) directs businesses to the Sales or business team for case-by-case pricing. Import-flow pricing depends on the payment methods, FX, taxes, settlement currency and business eligibility. Export-card rates do not automatically apply to this separate product.


Similarly, the standard[payment gateway](https://razorpay.com/payment-gateway/) , international cards and MoneySaver collection account have different purposes. A domestic welcome offer does not determine your international charges.


## Which RBI and FEMA Rules Matter to the Comparison?


RBI’s 2025 payment-aggregator directions set a maximum ₹25 lakh per transaction for inward or outward transactions processed by a PA-CB. The rule should be applied to the relevant flow, rather than described as either a universal cross-border cap or no cap at all.


The framework excludes certain card-network FX-settlement flows in which the aggregator receives local currency, and banks acting in that role do not need separate PA authorisation. The provider’s legal entity and the payment flow determine the applicable rules. A direct AD-bank arrangement is a separate route for suitable receipts; splitting a transaction does not remove regulatory obligations. See Razorpay’s[PA-CB explanation](https://razorpay.com/blog/razorpay-rbi-pa-cb-licence-international-payments/) for the entity and direction checks.


The amended FEMA 2026 regulations, in force since 1 October 2026, generally provide nine months from shipment for goods or invoice date for services, with twelve months where the export is invoiced and/or settled in INR. Specific export categories and AD-bank extensions have their own provisions. An INR credit after conversion does not automatically establish eligibility for the longer period.


Services EDF is generally due within 30 days after invoice month-end. A consolidated monthly declaration is permitted, not compulsory, and the regulations include alternative provisions and extensions. The filing process depends on the export category and any permitted extension. These obligations are separate from the provider’s settlement cycle.


## Does Payment Performance Change the Cost Decision?


Processing cost matters alongside legitimate completed sales. For card checkout, compare actual captured value, permitted recovery, fees and risk outcomes. A declined attempt is uncollected at that moment; the same order may later succeed through an allowed retry or another method.


Do not multiply attempted value by a count-based approval rate unless ticket sizes and capture assumptions justify it. Review both counts and values, distinguish authorisation from capture, and avoid calling net receipts profit. For invoiced bank transfers, assess collection completion and customer convenience rather than applying a card-authorisation benchmark.


## Which Method Fits Your Business?


- **Smaller invoices:** check minimum charges and whether a card-based percentage fee produces a smaller deduction.
- **Invoiced B2B receipts:** assess bank-transfer collection, invoice requirements, actual FX and settlement conditions.
- **Online consumer purchases:** retain a suitable checkout experience and compare eligible card-payment performance.
- **Recurring subscriptions:** verify the recurring-billing product, supported countries and payment methods separately.
- **Foreign-currency needs:** an eligible EEFC arrangement supports permitted foreign-currency retention; a collection account is not an unrestricted holding account.


> **Did You Know?** Zero stated FX markup does not mean the payment is free. A separate processing fee, an applicable minimum and GST can still reduce the net amount received.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### Is Razorpay bank transfer always cheaper than its card option?


No universal result follows from the headline rates. Invoice size, any flat charge, actual FX, account terms and the customer’s ability to use the method matter. The ₹33,333 crossover above applies only to its stated model assumptions.


### How do I calculate the cost of a USD 1,000 payment?


Convert the actual foreign amount using the documented applied rate, then deduct the applicable processing charge, GST and other disclosed costs. If ₹95,000 is the fee base and a 3% fee plus 18% GST applies, fee and tax total ₹3,363. Any different FX or tariff changes the result.


### Does net INR divided by the USD amount reveal FX markup?


No. It reveals a net receipt rate that includes fees, tax and adjustments. Use gross conversion before deductions to isolate the applied exchange rate, and compare it with a same-time reference.


### Does the ₹25 lakh rule apply to every international bank payment?


The cited maximum applies to inward or outward transactions processed by a PA-CB. Other regulatory flows, including relevant card-network exceptions and direct bank arrangements, require their own assessment.


### Does the 0% domestic welcome offer cover international collections?


The domestic 0% welcome offer does not cover international collections. International payments have their own processing fees, FX treatment, minimum charges, taxes and optional-service terms.
